title: Feasibility and safety of cellular therapy for in-utero repair of myelomeningocele (CuRe Trial): a first-in-human, phase 1, single-arm study
summary: Surgeons at UC Davis applied allogeneic human placenta-derived mesenchymal stem cells directly onto the exposed spinal cord during standard fetal surgery for six fetuses with severe spina bifida (myelomeningocele). All six children were born with intact repairs, no cell-related adverse effects, and reversal of the hindbrain herniation typically associated with the condition. It is the first time a live cellular therapy has been delivered in utero, and the results support advancing to a larger phase 1/2a cohort.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and thelancet.com: no retractions, corrections, or PubPeer threads found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Randomized phase 2b dose-escalation trial of stem cell therapy with laromestrocel for aging frailty
summary: In a 148-person randomized trial, a single IV infusion of allogeneic bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (laromestrocel) produced dose- and time-dependent gains in 6-minute-walk distance versus placebo in adults aged 70-85 with clinical frailty, with the largest doses adding roughly 63 meters at 9 months. It is among the largest controlled trials to date testing an off-the-shelf allogeneic cell therapy against a hallmark of biological aging rather than a single disease.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and cell.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24. Note: the independent commentary site 'The Niche' (Paul Knoepfler, March 2026) raised methodological questions about an unexplained decline in the placebo group's walk-test scores between months 3 and 9, and criticized overselling in accompanying press coverage -- this is post-publication commentary, not a peer-reviewed correction.

title: Stem-Cell-Derived Biologic Ventricular Assist Tissue in Heart Failure
summary: In the ongoing BioVAT-HF trial, 20 patients with advanced heart failure received an implanted patch of induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived engineered heart muscle sewn onto the epicardium. At 3 months the grafts thickened the treated heart wall by 4.5 mm and improved ejection fraction and quality-of-life scores, with benefits partly sustained out to 36 months in long-term follow-up. It is one of the first controlled trials showing an iPSC-derived tissue graft can measurably remuscularize a failing human heart.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nejm.org: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Daraxonrasib or Chemotherapy in Previously Treated Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer
summary: The phase 3 RASolute 302 trial randomized patients with previously treated metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to daraxonrasib, an oral pan-RAS(ON) inhibitor, or standard chemotherapy. Daraxonrasib nearly doubled median overall survival (13.2 vs 6.7 months, hazard ratio 0.40) along with improved progression-free survival, a magnitude of benefit described by investigators as unprecedented for this cancer. Dermatologic toxicity and emerging resistance via KRAS amplification and other pathway alterations remain open challenges.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nejm.org: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour
summary: The International Brain Laboratory, a 12-lab consortium, recorded from more than 600,000 neurons across 279 brain regions in 139 mice performing a decision-making task, producing the first standardized, brain-wide activity atlas of its kind. Task-related and movement-related signals were found to be far more broadly distributed across the brain than prior single-region studies suggested. The underlying dataset and pipeline are openly released, and the finding has already reshaped how the field designs region-specific versus brain-wide circuit studies.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nature.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2
summary: Evo 2 is a 40-billion-parameter DNA foundation model trained on over 9 trillion nucleotides spanning all domains of life, capable of predicting variant effects and generating synthetic genomic sequences from DNA to RNA to protein. Arc Institute and collaborators showed it can classify pathogenic mutations zero-shot and design functional genetic elements without task-specific fine-tuning. It has become one of the most widely used open genomic foundation models since its 2025 preprint release, though independent benchmarks have since identified specific blind spots.

title: Restoring rapid natural bimanual typing with a neuroprosthesis after paralysis
summary: BrainGate investigators built an intracortical brain-computer interface that decodes attempted finger movements on a QWERTY layout, letting two participants -- one with ALS, one with a cervical spinal cord injury -- type at up to 22 words per minute with a 1.6% word error rate, approaching able-bodied typing accuracy. This is a substantial throughput jump over prior hand-motor intracortical BCI decoders and moves implanted typing interfaces closer to practical, everyday communication for people with paralysis.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nature.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Patient-Specific In Vivo Gene Editing to Treat a Rare Genetic Disease
summary: A CHOP/Penn team designed, manufactured, and administered a bespoke in vivo CRISPR base-editing therapy for an infant ("KJ") with life-threatening carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency in under six months, using lipid nanoparticles to deliver a base editor targeted to his specific mutation. After two infusions the child tolerated substantially more dietary protein and a lower dose of nitrogen-scavenger medication with no serious adverse events. It is the first published case of a fully individualized, patient-specific gene-editing drug, though it is a single-patient case study and experts have flagged open questions about manufacturing scalability and regulatory pathways for replicating the approach.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nejm.org: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Vascular network-inspired diffusible scaffolds for engineering functional midbrain organoids
summary: Standard neural organoids suffer necrotic, hypoxic cores because nutrients and oxygen can only diffuse in from the surface. This group 3D-printed vascular-network-inspired diffusible (VID) scaffolds -- meshed tubular channel networks -- into culture wells, letting midbrain organoids grow with far less necrosis and hypoxia, along with better dopaminergic neuron maturation, more complex network activity, and more physiologically realistic drug responses. It's a low-tech, broadly adoptable alternative to microfluidic or vascularized-implant approaches for solving organoid diffusion limits.

title: Distinct in vivo dynamics of donor-derived stem cell memory CAR T cells post-allogeneic HSCT relapse
summary: Researchers co-led by Luca Gattinoni and James Kochenderfer engineered CAR T cells that acquire a stem-cell-memory (TSCM) phenotype and tested them in a first-in-human trial in patients relapsing after allogeneic stem cell transplant. The TSCM-phenotype CAR T cells expanded and persisted markedly better than conventional CAR T products, driving complete responses at doses as low as 250,000 cells/kg without lymphodepleting chemotherapy beforehand. Lower effective doses and no chemo preconditioning could translate into a substantially safer, less toxic CAR-T regimen if the results hold up in larger cohorts.

title: Human embryonic stem cell-derived dopaminergic cells for Parkinson's disease: a phase 1/2 open-label trial
summary: In this first-in-human European trial, researchers transplanted dopamine-producing neurons grown from human embryonic stem cells directly into the brains of eight people with moderate Parkinson's disease. After 12 months of follow-up under immunosuppression, the cell product caused no serious product-related adverse events and no graft-induced dyskinesia, a major feasibility milestone for replacing the neurons lost in Parkinson's disease with lab-grown cells. One of eight participants died from an unrelated pulmonary infection during follow-up, not attributed to the cell product. The trial is among the first pluripotent stem-cell therapies for Parkinson's approved for clinical testing in Europe.

title: Enhancer-directed gene delivery for digit regeneration based on conserved epidermal factors
summary: Comparing regenerating zebrafish fins, salamander limbs, and mouse digit tips, researchers found that the transcription factors SP6 and SP8 act as a conserved genetic switch in wound skin that drives appendage regrowth, and that removing them blocks bony digit-tip regeneration in mice. They then packaged an AAV gene therapy carrying a zebrafish-derived regeneration enhancer to deliver FGF8, a downstream SP target, directly to amputation wounds, partially restoring regeneration in SP-deficient mice and accelerating it in normal mice. It is an early proof-of-concept for injury-site-specific gene therapy that could one day help regrow lost digit or limb tissue.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

title: Physiology and immunology of a pig-to-human decedent kidney xenotransplant
summary: Surgeons transplanted a minimally gene-edited pig kidney into a brain-dead human maintained on a ventilator for a pre-planned 61-day study, the longest such xenotransplant physiology study to date. The kidney sustained hemodynamic and electrolyte stability and dialysis independence for weeks; antibody-mediated rejection emerged around day 33 but was fully reversed with plasma exchange, complement inhibition, and anti-thymocyte globulin. The study demonstrates both the promise and the immunological hurdles of pig-to-human kidney xenotransplantation as a potential answer to the organ-donor shortage.

title: Sacituzumab Govitecan plus Pembrolizumab for Advanced Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
summary: This international phase 3 trial (443 patients across 186 sites in 28 countries) tested whether adding the antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab govitecan to the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab works better than standard chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab as first-line treatment for PD-L1-positive metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The combination cut the risk of progression or death by 35% (median progression-free survival 11.2 vs. 7.8 months) with a higher response rate and fewer treatment discontinuations. The FDA approved the combination in June 2026 based on these results, making it a likely new standard of care for this aggressive cancer subtype.

title: Efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide 14 mg (flexible dose) in early-stage symptomatic Alzheimer's disease (evoke and evoke+): two phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials
summary: Two identically designed phase 3 trials tested whether once-daily oral semaglutide (the active ingredient in Ozempic/Wegovy) could slow Alzheimer's progression in 3,808 adults with amyloid-confirmed early-stage disease, followed for up to 156 weeks across 566 sites in 40 countries. Despite strong hope from observational and diabetes-trial data suggesting GLP-1 drugs protect the brain, semaglutide showed no benefit over placebo on cognitive or functional decline, though it did significantly lower CSF biomarkers of tau pathology and neuroinflammation. The dissociation between biomarker activity and clinical benefit is a high-profile negative result for one of the most-hyped drug classes in medicine.

title: Neuroproteasomes regulate endogenous tau paired helical filament formation in an APOE genotype- and age-dependent manner
summary: Researchers discovered that neurons have a specialized proteasome embedded in their plasma membrane, dubbed a 'neuroproteasome', that normally keeps the Alzheimer's-linked protein tau from misfolding. Using a novel cell-impermeant inhibitor, they showed that blocking this neuroproteasome rapidly causes normal tau to misfold into paired helical filaments, the same structures found in Alzheimer's brains. The APOE4 gene variant, the strongest genetic Alzheimer's risk factor, reduces neuroproteasome levels at the membrane by about a third, while the protective APOE2 variant nearly doubles them, offering a mechanistic bridge between genetic risk, aging, and the onset of tau pathology.

title: Advancing regulatory variant effect prediction with AlphaGenome
summary: DeepMind's AlphaGenome is a unified deep-learning model that reads up to one million base pairs of DNA and predicts thousands of molecular readouts, including gene expression, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, transcription-factor binding, 3D chromatin contacts, and splicing, at single-base resolution. It matches or beats specialized state-of-the-art models in 25 of 26 variant-effect benchmarks, and the authors show it can simultaneously explain multiple mechanisms behind clinically relevant mutations near the TAL1 oncogene. It is a discriminative regulatory-genomics model, distinct from generative sequence-design models such as Evo 2.

title: A neuroprosthesis for restoring hand movement and sensation in a person with complete tetraplegia
summary: Researchers built a 'double neural bypass', a hybrid brain-computer interface that reads intracortical signals related to movement intent and uses AI to drive electrical stimulation of the spinal cord and forearm muscles, restoring real-time hand grasp in a man with complete C4/C5 tetraplegia. Sensors on a hand orthosis simultaneously feed pressure data back into the sensory cortex via intracortical microstimulation, restoring a sense of touch. Over three years, the participant regained the ability to self-feed and grasp objects, with lasting gains in arm strength and tactile sensitivity even when the device was switched off, suggesting the system induced genuine neuroplasticity years after his injury.

title: Human microphysiological systems of aging recreate the in vivo process expediting evaluation of anti-geronic strategies
summary: Bioengineers built a human iPSC-derived organ-on-chip system linking engineered white-adipose and liver tissue, then perfused it with blood serum from older versus younger human donors. Within four days, serum from older donors induced chronic inflammation, impaired glucose regulation, disrupted fat metabolism, and cellular senescence, hallmarks that normally take decades to develop in people, while young serum reversed some of these changes. The system is proposed as a fast, human-relevant platform for testing anti-aging interventions without waiting years for results.

title: Prime Editing for p47phox-Deficient Chronic Granulomatous Disease
summary: This paper reports the first peer-reviewed clinical use of prime editing, a 'search-and-replace' gene-editing technology that corrects mutations without cutting both DNA strands, in human patients. Two patients with p47phox-deficient chronic granulomatous disease, a severe inherited immune disorder, received an infusion of their own blood stem cells corrected with the prime editor PM359. Both patients showed restored NADPH oxidase immune activity within one month, sustained through 4-6 months of follow-up, with no clinically significant treatment-related adverse events.
